questions.topic: Wind operating regions and curtailed output
questions.learningObjective: Identify the operating region in which wind turbine output rises with wind speed
questions.stem: During a revision session, Priya sketches the wind speed range over which a turbine produces power and marks three speeds: cut-in, rated and cut-out. What does the region between cut-in and rated represent?

options.text: The region where output rises with wind speed, from zero at cut-in to the rating at rated speed
The region in which the machine is deliberately held idle to protect the gearbox from high winds
options.misconception: treats the part-load region as a deliberate shutdown

options.text: The region above which the blades are feathered and the turbine stops generating entirely
options.misconception: confuses the part-load region with the shutdown region

options.text: The region in which the output is capped at the nameplate rating regardless of how strong the wind is
options.misconception: describes the above-rated region, not the part-load region

questions.explanation: Between cut-in and rated speed the turbine runs and its output climbs with the wind. Above rated speed output is held at the nameplate value, and above cut-out the machine shuts down.
questions.hint: Output is still climbing in that region, not capped.

options.text: The comparison is missing the moisture content of the fuel, which determines how much heat it actually gives
options.misconception: introduces a fuel property the argument never turned on

options.text: The comparison is missing the transport distance, so the saving could be used up by hauling the fuel
options.misconception: adds a plausible but unstated logistics factor

options.text: The comparison is missing the carbon payback, since disturbed land and soil carbon take years to repay
Nothing is missing, since a lower stack emission is enough to show the fuel is better for the climate

options.misconception: assumes a shared final step implies equal energy use

options.text: That the ore route is the only one that produces metal fit for structural use
options.misconception: invents a quality limit that does not exist

options.text: The scrap route skips the refining steps that dominate the energy use of primary metal

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Round-trip efficiency of storage
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of a storage unit's round-trip efficiency
questions.stem: A study group wants to measure the round-trip efficiency of a battery storage unit installed beside a solar array. Describe the measurement.

answer.exemplar: The group would record the electricity drawn by the charging circuit over a set of complete cycles and the electricity returned by the discharging circuit, using the meter on each side separately rather than a single house meter. Both sets of readings must cover the same energy going in and out, so the meter readings are paired by time and the discharge periods are matched to the charge periods. The ratio of energy delivered to energy stored gives the round-trip efficiency, and repeating the test over several days captures what happens when the battery is partly charged or held at a different temperature.

questions.explanation: A round-trip figure needs energy in and out measured on the same boundary, so meters belong on both sides. Matching periods and repeating the test captures temperature and partial-charge effects.
questions.hint: Meter both sides of the unit over the same cycles.

stimulus.body: Question 6 states that a heat pump rated at 12 kW of output consumed 3 kW of electricity over one test hour. Question 7 states that a diesel generator rated at 100 kW produced 62 kWh of electricity across a full day of intermittent running.

questions.stem: Based on the worksheet, what does the information support about the two machines?

options.text: That the heat pump delivered four times the power it consumed in that hour, a figure from one test point
That the generator ran at sixty-two per cent of its rating all day, since that is its output over its rating
options.misconception: treats daily energy over power as a utilisation percentage

options.text: That the generator is more efficient, since it produced sixty-two kilowatt hours from a smaller rating
options.misconception: compares energy over a day with power over an hour

options.misconception: confuses power with energy as if interchangeable

questions.explanation: Dividing the heat pump's output by its input gives four for the hour, a point measurement not a seasonal figure. The generator's daily energy over its rating is no percentage: power and energy differ.
questions.hint: Separate a point measurement from a whole-period figure.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Infiltration and envelope conductance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why draughts add to the heat loss of a room
questions.stem: Explain to the group why a room with old single glazing and constant window draughts can use more gas than its floor area alone would suggest.

answer.exemplar: Heat loss depends on the area of each surface and on its conductance, so a room's floor area is only one term in the total. Single-glazed windows have a much higher conductance than the walls, and every open window or missing seal adds an uncontrolled flow of outside air that has to be heated. Both effects scale with the cold of the weather rather than with the floor area, so a draughty room on a cold day can demand far more gas than its size suggests, and the fix is a better envelope rather than a bigger boiler.

questions.explanation: Heat loss runs through the envelope and through uncontrolled air flow, and neither is fixed by floor area. Older glazing raises conductive loss while draughts add a ventilation loss scaled by weather.
questions.hint: Losses come through surfaces and draughts, not area alone.

questions.stem: A wind farm's output log shows turbines producing at full rating for hours while the grid operator reduces their dispatch. How should the study group describe the lost energy?

options.text: As a technical fault, since a healthy turbine cannot sit at its rating without generating more
options.misconception: reads a dispatch limit as an equipment malfunction

options.text: As curtailed output, energy the wind made available that the grid could not accept at that moment
As a turbine availability failure, since curtailed machines are not considered available
options.misconception: confuses grid curtailment with turbine downtime

options.text: As unnecessary loss, since a modern grid can always absorb any amount of wind generation
options.misconception: assumes the grid has unlimited capacity for wind output

questions.explanation: Curtailment happens when the network cannot accept the power offered, so the turbines are healthy and the wind is present but the energy is not taken. It is a system constraint, not a fault.
questions.hint: The energy existed; something stopped it being used.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Round-trip efficiency of storage
questions.learningObjective: Design a fair comparison of two storage technologies
questions.stem: Two storage technologies are to be compared on the same site. Describe how the study group would compare their round-trip efficiencies.

answer.exemplar: The group would put a meter on the charging side and another on the discharging side of each unit and run both through identical charge and discharge schedules, so that the same quantity of energy enters and leaves in each case. Each unit would be cycled several times and the tests repeated at different states of charge, since a unit that is only partly charged or nearly full does not behave like one cycled from empty to full. The ratio of energy delivered to energy taken in would then be compared directly, with the instrumentation accuracy recorded so that small differences are not overstated.

questions.explanation: A fair comparison needs the same energy in and out for each unit, with meters on both sides so internal losses are included. Repeating at different states of charge stops edge effects deciding it.
questions.hint: Same energy in, same energy out, meters on both sides.

questions.hint: Compare what each consumed, not just what it delivered.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Infiltration and envelope conductance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why glazing replacement reduces heat loss
questions.stem: Explain why replacing a draughty old window with a sealed double-glazed unit can cut the gas bill even though the room's floor area and volume stay the same.

answer.exemplar: Heat leaves a room through its surfaces and through the air that leaks in and out, and the bill depends on how fast that happens when the outside is colder than the inside. A double-glazed unit has a much lower conductance than single glazing, and sealing the frame removes the draught that was dragging cold air in and warming it inside the room. The heat loss is then roughly proportional to the new conductance times the area times the temperature difference, and with a smaller factor the same room needs less gas for the same comfort.

questions.explanation: The bill follows heat loss, which depends on conductance and uncontrolled air flow as much as on area. A sealed double-glazed unit lowers conductance and removes the draught, so less gas is needed.
questions.hint: The factor that changed is conductance, not floor area.

questions.topic: Round-trip efficiency of storage
questions.learningObjective: Design an estimate of round-trip efficiency from operating data
questions.stem: Round-trip efficiency has to be estimated from operating data rather than by instrumenting the plant. Describe how the study group would do this for a pumped hydro scheme.

answer.exemplar: The group would take the electricity exported to the grid during pumping, which is recorded at the generator, and the electricity drawn from the grid during generating, recorded at the pump, and pair the figures by period so that the same stored volume is accounted for in each case. Where the scheme has a pumped and a generated mode in the same period, the net energy for that period is taken directly. The ratio of the exported energy to the imported energy gives the round-trip efficiency, and the scheme's own balance of plant and standby losses should be noted as a source of difference from published figures.

questions.explanation: The scheme must be measured on a boundary including both pump and generator, so no stage is left out of the ratio. Pairing periods keeps the same stored energy on both sides.
questions.hint: Put the pump and generator on the same measurement boundary.

questions.topic: Infiltration and envelope conductance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rated insulation value does not describe a built wall
questions.stem: A second claim troubles the group too, that a new building's walls are twice as good as the old ones. Explain why it needs care.

answer.exemplar: The claim usually rests on a nominal u-value that describes heat flow through a panel of the material in a laboratory test. A real wall is made of several layers with joints, fixings and voids, and the way it is built and sealed determines how close the finished wall comes to its rated figure. Air leakage through the frame, service penetrations and the extraction system can dominate the remaining loss, so a halving of the panel figure does not translate into a halving of the bill.

questions.explanation: A rated u-value describes a panel under test conditions, while a built wall adds joints, fixings, voids and air leakage the rating does not capture. Halving the panel figure need not halve losses.
questions.hint: A rated value describes a panel, not a finished wall.

answer.exemplar: The group would record the street's half-hourly electricity demand at the incoming service for a week with the battery absent, establishing the shape and size of the evening peak. The battery would then be installed and charged deliberately from midday, when demand is low, and discharged to cover the peak in the same house, so the change in the street profile could be read directly from the meters. Comparing the two weeks on a like-for-like weekday basis, and correcting for any difference in weather, would show whether the peak was actually reduced or merely shifted.

questions.topic: Infiltration and envelope conductance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why conductance and air change rate must be treated separately
questions.stem: Explain why a study group should treat the air change rate of a room as a separate calculation from the conductance of its glazing.

answer.exemplar: Conductance describes heat flow through a surface of given area at a given temperature difference, and it is a property of the construction. Air change rate describes how much outside air is drawn in and expelled each hour, and it is governed by the leaks, the extract fan and the doors being opened. The two can be traded against each other, since tightening the envelope makes a given air change rate cost more to heat, while a higher air change rate undoes the benefit of good glazing, so a plan that improves only one of them can achieve very little.

questions.explanation: Conductance and air change rate act on the same heat loss by different routes, so improving one can cancel the other. Tightening the glazing while the extract runs loses much of the benefit.
questions.hint: The two routes act on one loss and can cancel one another.

answer.exemplar: The group would meter the grid connection on both the import and the export side, record the battery's state of charge throughout, and log ambient temperature at the unit. The unit would then be run through a set of real patterns, including charging on sunny days at low demand, discharging into the evening peak, and sitting idle overnight, with the manufacturer test repeated alongside for comparison. questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rated value and a room's real loss can diverge
questions.stem: Quoted insulation values and the heat a room really loses can point in different directions. Explain to the group why.

answer.exemplar: The quoted value describes heat flow through a panel of the material under test conditions, with no joints, fixings or leaks included. The room's real loss depends on the whole assembly, on how it was built, on the air that leaks through the frame and on the extract system running. A wall with a good rating in a leaky room can therefore lose more heat overall than a poorer wall in a tight one, because the air path and the fabric path add together, and the room that feels draughtier is often the one with the worse walls.

questions.explanation: A quoted value describes a panel under laboratory conditions, while real loss depends on the built assembly and air leakage. The two paths add, so a good wall in a leaky room can lose more.
questions.hint: The panel value ignores joints, leaks and the extract.

answer.exemplar: The group would fit a meter to the battery's connection and log both the power flowing and the battery's state of charge through a normal week of household use, including the evening peak and the following overnight recharge. The energy discharged to the house, the energy drawn from the grid to recharge it, and the energy still stored at the end of the period would all be recorded, so the usable fraction is measured against what was actually put in rather than against the nameplate capacity. questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why recycled aluminium needs less energy
questions.learningObjective: Read a flow chart that marks the energy input of a route
questions.stem: One flow chart shows scrap aluminium entering a sorting step, then a furnace, then a casting step, with a heat input marked at the furnace. What does it tell the group?

options.text: That the sorting step is the most energy-hungry part of the recycled route
options.misconception: assigns the dominant energy demand to the wrong step

options.text: That the recycled route's energy demand is concentrated in one step, rather than spread across several
That the casting step consumes more energy than the furnace, since casting comes last
options.misconception: infers energy from sequence position

options.text: That the chart is incomplete, since no material leaves the furnace, so the route cannot be mass balanced
options.misconception: objects to an omission the chart does not make

questions.explanation: Marking the heat input at one step shows the recycled route concentrates its energy demand there, unlike the primary route's refining and electrolysis. Any estimate of its energy rests on that figure.
questions.hint: One marked heat input means one dominant step.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Round-trip efficiency of storage
questions.learningObjective: Design a test that separates pipe losses from turbine losses
questions.stem: Losses in a pumped hydro scheme have to be attributed between the pipes and the turbines. Describe how the study group would do that.

answer.exemplar: The group would instrument the upper and lower reservoirs with level sensors and flow meters, so that the volume of water moved can be measured independently of the electrical meters on the pump and the generator. The hydraulic energy available from the stored head can then be compared with the electrical energy the pump puts in and the generator takes out, and the discrepancy is the part lost in pipes, valves and leakage. Repeating the measurement at different head levels and flow rates shows whether the loss is roughly fixed, which points to leakage, or proportional to flow, which points to friction.

questions.explanation: Level and flow meters give the hydraulic energy independently of electrical meters, so the difference isolates pipe and valve losses. Repeating at different flows separates leakage from friction.
questions.hint: Measure the water's energy directly, then compare it.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Rated against seasonal efficiency
questions.learningObjective: Convert a seasonal energy total into full-output hours

stimulus.body: Item 14 states that a ground source heat pump has a rated output of 40 kW and a seasonal coefficient of performance of 3.6. Item 15 states that the same installation supplied 91 440 kWh of heat over the year while consuming 25 400 kWh of electricity.

questions.stem: What do these two items allow the group to conclude?

options.text: That the unit delivered its full rated output for 2 286 hours of the year
options.misconception: misreads the heat delivered as hours of full operation

options.text: That the unit ran at its rated output for the whole of the heating season
options.misconception: assumes a seasonal coefficient implies running at rating

options.text: That the unit ran at close to its rated output for about 2 286 hours of the year
That the unit's seasonal coefficient of performance of 3.6 cannot be reconciled with the annual figures
options.misconception: claims the figures are inconsistent when they agree

questions.explanation: The year's heat over the rated output gives the full-output hours: 91 440 over 40 is 2 286. The heat over the electricity confirms the coefficient of 3.6. The rating is a peak, not the average.
questions.hint: Divide the year's heat by the rated output for the hours.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Infiltration and envelope conductance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why draughts persist in a well-insulated house
questions.stem: A draughty room in a well-insulated house can still be uncomfortable and expensive to heat. Explain to the group why.

answer.exemplar: Insulation reduces heat loss through the fabric, but the air entering through gaps is warmed inside the room and then lost again, and that loss is governed by how much outside air is brought in rather than by the conductance of the walls. In a draughty room the extract system pulls through a large volume of cold air, and every cubic metre of it must be heated, so the room can be cold and costly even though the fabric is good. The fix is to reduce the air path, or to supply the incoming air already warmed, not simply to add more insulation.

questions.explanation: Fabric losses and ventilation losses respond to different measures, so good insulation does little about cold air entering through gaps. The remedy is to reduce the air path or heat the incoming air.
questions.hint: Insulation touches one path; the draught is another.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Wind operating regions and curtailed output
questions.learningObjective: State what a capacity factor measures
questions.stem: A revision note says that a wind farm's annual output divided by its rated power and the hours in the year gives its capacity factor. What does that quantity measure?

options.text: The proportion of the year's energy the farm could have produced had the wind never stopped
options.misconception: describes a counterfactual, not the utilisation figure

options.text: The proportion of the time the blades spent turning at full speed
options.misconception: conflates the capacity factor with time at rated output

options.text: The efficiency of the conversion from wind to electricity, which the figure also captures
options.misconception: treats utilisation as a conversion efficiency

options.text: The share of the maximum possible energy the farm actually delivered over the period

questions.explanation: The capacity factor compares what was delivered with the largest energy the rating could produce over the same hours, so it measures how fully the site was used, not turbine efficiency.
questions.hint: Delivered energy against the maximum the rating allows.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Water withdrawal against water consumption
questions.learningObjective: Compare the water behaviour of a mill and a thermal station
questions.stem: A table lists a textile mill at 1 200 cubic metres per day withdrawn and 300 consumed, and a thermal power station at 3 600 withdrawn and 3 100 consumed. What does the table support?

options.text: That both draw heavily on their sources, but the mill returns a much larger share of what it takes
That the mill is more wasteful, since it withdraws three times as much water
options.misconception: calls a larger withdrawal wasteful without a service basis

options.text: That the power station's consumption is unacceptably high, since it exceeds the mill's by a factor of ten
options.misconception: judges absolute consumption without any service comparison

options.text: That the mill and the station draw from the same water body, since both withdraw in the thousands
options.misconception: infers a common source from the magnitude of the numbers

questions.explanation: The mill consumes 300 of 1 200 cubic metres, returning the rest, while the station consumes 3 100 of 3 600, passing most on as waste heat. Both take large volumes; the difference reflects the process.
questions.hint: Compare consumption with withdrawal for each system.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Stack measurement against the full chain
questions.learningObjective: Calculate annual process emissions from a unit factor
questions.stem: A paper mill's process emits 0.9 tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne of pulp produced. For a year in which the mill produces 180 000 tonnes of pulp, what is the process emission in tonnes of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Emission per tonne of product times the output gives the yearly total: 0.9 times 180 000 is 162 000 tonnes of carbon dioxide. That covers the process alone, not the fuel burned for heat.
questions.hint: Multiply the emission factor by the tonnes produced.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Bioenergy carbon payback and land use
questions.learningObjective: Critique a bioenergy claim that ignores land use change
questions.stem: A study group writes that bioenergy is better than coal because it releases less carbon dioxide at the stack and grows back every year. What is the weakness in the claim as stated?

options.text: It compares stack figures from plants that may use different fuels and cannot be compared
options.misconception: raises an irrelevant comparability worry

options.text: It ignores the carbon released when the land is cleared, which can outweigh the saving for decades
It assumes the biomass will actually be harvested, though some schemes leave it standing
options.misconception: raises an operational assumption the claim does not rely on

options.text: It ignores that coal plants also supply other products, so the comparison is not like for like
options.misconception: invents a co-product issue the claim does not turn on

questions.explanation: A lower stack figure and a regrowing crop say nothing about the carbon released when land is cleared for the plantation, a debt that can take decades to repay. The claim omits that history.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the land before the crop was planted.
